EMI in power converters primarily arises from switching of DC voltage using PWM signals.
Frequency modulation techniques spread harmonic energy over a frequency band, reducing peak EMI amplitude.
Spread Spectrum Frequency Modulation (SSFM) was originally developed for digital systems in the mid-1990s.
The modulation index m = Δf / f_c quantifies the relative frequency deviation in SSFM.
Carson’s rule estimates that 98% of the energy of a frequency-modulated signal lies within bandwidth B = 2(Δf + f_m).
Sinusoidal, triangular, and exponential modulation profiles produce different EMI spectral envelopes.
Triangular profiles with equal slopes for rising and falling intervals produce a flatter EMI spectrum envelope.
Exponential profiles allow selective attenuation at specific frequencies by adjusting concavity parameters.
Higher modulation indices increase EMI attenuation but risk overlapping harmonic bands.
Experimental tests used a buck converter with switching frequencies from 100 kHz to 1 MHz.
At 200 kHz switching frequency with sinusoidal modulation (m=6, f_m=10 kHz), peak EMI was reduced by about 10 dB.
At 1 MHz switching frequency, SSFM showed better EMI reduction due to less harmonic band overlap.
Triangular modulation profile yielded the highest overall EMI reduction in experiments.
Exponential profile was less sensitive to harmonic overlap and better for selective frequency cancellation.
Operating the converter in open loop with fixed duty cycle ensured EMI changes were due to frequency modulation only.
A resolution bandwidth of 9 kHz was used for EMI measurements to capture spread spectrum effects.
Frequency modulation can be random, chaotic, or deterministic; deterministic periodic profiles allow frequency-selective EMI control.
Overlap of spread bands in higher harmonics reduces SSFM effectiveness if parameters are not optimized.
The study experimentally validated theoretical predictions of EMI reduction using SSFM.
The choice of modulation profile depends on application requirements for overall EMI reduction or selective frequency attenuation.
